etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 巡(まわ)り (mawari, “going around”, honorific suffix) + さん (-san)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English America, from New Latin America, feminine form of Americus, a Latinization of the given name of Amerigo Vespucci (1451-1512), an Italian explorer.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English cassette, ultimately from French cassette.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 一(いち) (ichi, “one”) + 体(たい) (-tai, counter for bodies and humanoid objects).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 乗(の)り (nori) + 物(もの) (-mono)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 勝(かっ)手(て) (katte) + に (ni).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare なか (naka, “middle, inside”). Likely ultimately from Proto-Japonic *naka.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 原料 (MC ngjwon lew): 原 (gen, “original”) + 料 (ryō, “material”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ki₁mi₁⟩ → */kʲimʲi/ → /kimi/
From Old Japanese. Possibly a borrowing from the Sillan word for king, written with the character 今 (kum). The same morpheme survives in the second syllable of the Modern Korean word 임금 (imgeum).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The kimi changes to gimi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 君 (MC kjun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kimud͡ʑi/ → /kind͡ʑi/
Shift from older きむぢ (kimudi → kimuji).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 図(ず) (zu, “diagram”) + 表(ひょう) (hyō, “table”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *paka. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Ultimate derivation unknown. One possibility is that the final ka may be 処(か) (-ka, suffix denoting place), as in the term 住(す)み処(か) (sumika, “dwelling, home, abode”, literally “living place”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 墓 (MC muH). Compare modern Min Nan readings bō͘, bōng.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from tozuku below.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *tontoku.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 市 (ichi). Found in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Uncertain. Possibly from Middle Chinese 年度 (MC nen duH). Compare modern Mandarin 年度 (niándù).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *isonku. Appears to be root iso ("earnest? industrious?") + verb-forming suffix -gu of uncertain meaning. Cognate with archaic adjective 勤し (isoshi, “diligent, industrious, hard-working”) and modern verb 勤しむ (isoshimu, “to work diligently, industriously”), may also be related to adverb いそいそ (isoiso, “cheerfully, unreservedly”), verb 勇む (isamu, “to be in high spirits, to be encouraged”).
First attested as noun form isogi ("hurrying, rushing") in the Man'yōshū of 759.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Further derivation unknown.
First attested in a piece of 催馬楽 (saibara, “court music”) dated to the late 600s, early 700s.
Homophonic verb 跨ぐ (matagu, “to straddle, to step across”) is likely a derivation of this verb, possibly from the idea of striding, i.e. walking quickly.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 憧る (akugaru).
Originally a compound of 所(あく) (aku) and 離(か)る (karu), the latter a cognate of 枯(か)れる (kareru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Doublet of 離す (hanasu, “to separate”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 毛(け) (ke, “fur, hair”) + 糸(いと) (ito, “thread, string”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 法 (MC pjop). Originally, the kan'on was はふ (fafu), and the goon was ほふ (fofu), although both became ほう (hō) in modern Japanese. It is suggested that the kan'on was used in the general senses, while the goon was used in Buddhist contexts.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French franc.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 毬 /球 (gjuw, “ball, sphere, orb”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Same word as 玉(たま) (tama, “ball, sphere, bullet, egg; gem, jewel, object of value”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Verbalization of 異 (koto, “difference”) + なる (naru, “the 連体形 (rentaikei, “adnominal form”) of なり (nari, “to be”)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle Chinese 智慧 (trjeᴴ hwejᴴ)
知 is a daiyōji replacing 智. 恵 is a daiyōji replacing 慧.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested in the Myōgoki (1275). According to one theory, the word is shortened from earlier attested 砂子 (sunago, “sand”); see there for more.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested in the Nihon Shoki (720). Some sources connect the initial isa- element to 石 (ishi, “stone”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Found in the Kojiki (712) in the name of the deity 須比智邇神 (supi₁di ni NO₂ KAMI₂, literally “god of the mud soil”). In most cases, the word has been conflated with 洲 (su, “sandbar”), which could be a cognate.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from written Chinese 綺麗, 奇麗 /绮丽, 奇丽. First attested in Japanese in the 1200s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Possibly the original form of mune below.
The first edition of the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten says that this is cognate with 棟 (muna, “main roofline, roof ridge”), from the underlying idea of central or main portion. However, see Etymology 2.
Possibly also related with 空, 虚 (muna, “emptiness, void”), from the idea of cavity.
Seldom used in isolation even in Old Japanese. Only found as the first element of compounds in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *munai. The apophony is similar to the phonetic process observed in the shift from 神 (kamu, “spirit, god”, older form used in compounds) to 神 (kami, newer form, used as a standalone noun); see WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.
Alternatively, may be a compound of 身 (mu, “body”) + 根 (ne, “root”). Other theories have been suggested.
The first edition of the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten says that this is cognate with 棟 (mune, “main roofline, roof ridge”) and 宗, 旨 (mune, “gist, main idea, primary part”), from the underlying idea of central or main portion. However, the accent of 胸 (mune) in the Heian period is HL, while the accent of 棟 (mune) is HH. This suggests that they may not be directly related.
Notably, 棟 and 宗 also have an older reading muna that is only used in compounds (for 宗, possibly only in place names). Meanwhile, 旨 (mune) (Heian HH) appears in The Tale of Genji of circa 1001-1004, and this reading is used as a standalone noun rather than in compounds. This is consistent with other nouns that have paired vowel forms, and suggests that muna is probably the original form, and that the compound derivation is a folk etymology.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 下二段 (shimo nidan) verb 茹づ (yuzu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese 行列 (MC haeng ljet). First attested in Japanese in 749.
The date of the mathematical sense is uncertain. Matrices for calculation were long known in Chinese mathematics, and were used to solve systems of linear equations in the work 九章算術 /九章算术 (“The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art”), compiled from the 10th through the 2nd centuries BCE. The component terms 行 and 列 (liè) are both used in that text, but not in the particular combination of 行列 (hángliè) (see also Wikisource). The first Japanese work on this aspect of mathematics was a 1683 text by 関孝和 (Seki Takakazu), but it is not yet clear if this text includes the term 行列 (gyōretsu) with the sense of matrix.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 見(み)る (miru, “to see, look”) + 慣(な)れる (nareru, “to get used to”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 酸(さん) (san, “acid”) + 性(せい) (-sei, “-ity”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 害 is a daiyōji replacing 碍.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/ʔiəm/ → /əmʉ/ → /omʉ/ → /oɴ/
From Middle Chinese 音 (MC 'im).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨oto₂⟩ → */otə/ → /oto/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ətə.
Appears in the late 1400s with the geminate pronunciation /otto/. This reading is very rare, and appears to have fallen out of use.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂⟩ → */tə/ → /to/
Apheresis of 音(おと) (oto) above.
The drop is likely due to lexicalization of compound terms (such as with the possessive particle の (no)), which would necessitate contraction of /CV oto/ to /CVto/ (e.g. no oto → noto) due to Old Japanese rules against vowel hiatus. This contracted form could have then been reanalyzed as a distinct form of the word.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ne₂⟩ → */nəɨ/ → /ne/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712, with the phonetic spelling 泥.
The original meaning appears to have been "a sound or cry, as made by an insect, bird, or beast", likely related to the verb for making such a sound, 鳴く (naku, “to make a sound; to cry out”), as well as its doublet 泣く (naku, “to cry, to weep”). It is also likely related to 鳴る (naru, “to sound; to ring”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 音 (MC 'im).
The kan'on pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing.
